course.title: AP U.S. History
course.description: Trace how Americans have argued over identity, power, work, and their place in the world, from the societies that existed before 1491 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Follow the nation's development from early contact and colonization through independence, civil war, industrialization, world wars, and recent decades.

unit.title: Period 4
unit.description: Follow the rise of party politics and a more participatory democracy, the market revolution, westward expansion and foreign policy, the Second Great Awakening and reform, and the growth of slavery from 1800 to 1848.

framework.name: Course themes
framework.title: Use the course themes to choose your evidence
framework.intro: The themes connect developments across all nine periods. A piece of evidence can fit more than one theme; choose the one that answers the prompt.
framework.sourceNote: Theme names, codes, and descriptions follow the AP U.S. History Course and Exam Description (fall 2026).

themes.title: American and National Identity
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why definitions of American and national identity and values have developed among the diverse and changing population of North America as well as on related topics, such as citizenship, constitutionalism, foreign policy, assimilation, and American exceptionalism.
themes.question: Who counted as American, and what did people believe the nation stood for?
themes.example: Debates over ratifying the Constitution turned on what kind of republic Americans wanted.

themes.title: Work, Exchange, and Technology
themes.description: This theme focuses on the factors behind the development of systems of economic exchange, particularly the role of technology, economic markets, and government.
themes.question: How did people earn a living, trade, and use new technology?
themes.example: Canals and railroads tied farmers in the West to markets in the East.

themes.title: Geography and the Environment
themes.description: This theme focuses on the role of geography and both the natural and human-made environments in the social and political developments in what would become the United States.
themes.question: How did land, climate, and resources shape choices, and how did people change them?
themes.example: The Chesapeake's climate suited tobacco, which shaped its labor system.

themes.title: Migration and Settlement
themes.description: This theme focuses on why and how the various people who moved to and within the United States both adapted to and transformed their new social and physical environments.
themes.question: Why did people move, and how did they change the places they settled?
themes.example: The Great Migration brought African Americans from the rural South to northern cities.

themes.title: Politics and Power
themes.description: This theme focuses on how different social and political groups have influenced society and government in the United States as well as how political beliefs and institutions have changed over time.
themes.question: Who held power, how did they use it, and who challenged it?
themes.example: The New Deal expanded the federal government's role in the economy.

themes.title: America in the World
themes.description: This theme focuses on the interactions between nations that affected North American history in the colonial period and on the influence of the United States on world affairs.
themes.question: How did contact, trade, diplomacy, and war connect America to other nations?
themes.example: The Seven Years' War left Britain in debt and changed its policies toward the colonies.

themes.title: American and Regional Culture
themes.description: This theme focuses on the how and why national, regional, and group cultures developed and changed as well as how culture has shaped government policy and the economy.
themes.question: How did beliefs, religion, arts, and media develop and shape public life?
themes.example: The Second Great Awakening inspired many Americans to join reform movements.

themes.title: Social Structures
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why systems of social organization develop and change as well as the impact that these systems have on the broader society.
themes.question: How were people ranked by race, class, and gender, and how did that change?
themes.example: The growth of a middle class in the Gilded Age changed ideas about leisure and family.

lesson.title: Jackson and Federal Power
lesson.summary: How Andrew Jackson's presidency divided Democrats and Whigs over the national bank, tariffs, and federal power, and how Indian removal shaped relations with American Indian nations.
learningGoals: Explain how Democrats and Whigs differed on the powers of the federal government.
Explain the causes and outcome of the nullification crisis and the Bank War.
Explain the causes and effects of American Indian removal.
lesson.bigIdea: Under Jackson, a mass electorate debated the powers of the federal government, and the federal government used its power to remove American Indian nations from the Southeast.
lesson.context: The CED asks you to explain the causes and effects of continuing policy debates about the role of the federal government. Pair each debate with the party and region that took each side.

sections.title: Democrats, Whigs, and the Bank War
sections.conceptTitle: Democrats, Whigs, and the Bank War

blocks.text: By the 1820s and 1830s, new political parties arose, the Democrats, led by Andrew Jackson, and the Whigs, led by Henry Clay, that disagreed about the role and powers of the federal government and issues such as the national bank, tariffs, and federally funded internal improvements. Democrats generally favored limited federal power, a more limited role for the national government in the economy, and the interests of farmers and workers. Whigs, who formed in opposition to what they called “King Andrew,” supported the American System of a national bank, a protective tariff, and federal funding of roads and canals.

Jackson's fight against the Second Bank of the United States showed the difference. Jackson saw the Bank as a monopoly that favored the wealthy. In 1832 he vetoed the bill to renew its charter, and he won reelection that year. He then removed federal deposits from the Bank and placed them in state banks, which critics called “pet banks.” A financial panic began in 1837, and it led to a depression that hurt the Democrats in the election of 1840.

sections.takeaway: Democrats and Whigs differed over the bank, tariffs, and internal improvements, and the Bank War made the divide sharper.

sections.title: The nullification crisis

blocks.text: Regional interests also shaped the federal power debate. Southerners disliked the protective tariffs of 1828 and 1832, which they thought raised the price of manufactured goods and favored the North. John C. Calhoun of South Carolina argued that a state could nullify, or declare void, a federal law that it judged unconstitutional. In November 1832 a South Carolina convention declared the tariffs null and void within the state.

Jackson rejected nullification as a threat to the Union and asked Congress to authorize force if needed. Congress passed the Force Act, and it also passed a compromise tariff in 1833 that lowered duties gradually. South Carolina then withdrew its nullification, though it also declared the Force Act null. The crisis ended without violence, but the question of whether states could resist federal law remained.

sections.takeaway: South Carolina's nullification challenge to the tariffs ended in a compromise but left the question of state authority unsettled.

sections.title: American Indian removal

blocks.text: Frontier settlers tended to champion expansion efforts, while American Indian resistance led to a sequence of wars and federal efforts to control and relocate American Indian populations. Settlers in Georgia, Alabama, and Mississippi wanted the land of the Cherokee, Creek, Choctaw, Chickasaw, and Seminole, even though several of these nations had adopted written constitutions, farming, and some American customs. Jackson, who had fought the Creek in 1814 and the Seminole in 1818, supported removal.

Congress passed the Indian Removal Act in 1830, which gave the president the power to exchange land west of the Mississippi River for Native land in the East. The Supreme Court ruled in Worcester v. Georgia (1832) that Georgia could not extend its laws over the Cherokee Nation, but the federal government did not enforce the decision. In 1835 a small group of Cherokee signed the Treaty of New Echota, which most of the nation rejected, and in 1838–1839 the army forced about 16,000 Cherokee westward on the Trail of Tears, on which thousands died. Other nations resisted, as in the Black Hawk War (1832) and the Second Seminole War (1835–1842).

blocks.title: Common trap
blocks.text: Removal was not carried out by settlers alone. The Indian Removal Act, treaties, and the army made it federal policy.

sections.takeaway: The federal government forced Native nations out of the Southeast through laws, treaties, and force.

connections.title: Democracy, expansion, and national identity
connections.body: Debates over power and territory happened alongside the growth of a national culture. Topic 4.9 follows that culture.
connections.transferQuestion: How did the nullification crisis show that regional interests could outweigh national loyalty?
connections.feedback: A strong answer notes that South Carolina placed its economic interest in lower tariffs ahead of the federal law, and that other Southern states did not support nullification.
